# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic meter of water weighs a thousand kilograms, and every liter that reaches a tenth-floor apartment must be lifted against gravity, pushed through miles of pipe, and delivered at a pressure that makes faucets work the way residents expect. Understanding how a city accomplishes this requires looking at elevation, energy, and the clever ways engineers have learned to manage both.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation Head

The core concept in water distribution is called "head," which is simply energy expressed as height. Water at an elevation of 100 meters above sea level contains potential energy relative to any point below it. If you have a reservoir on a hill 50 meters above a neighborhood, gravity alone will push water down to that neighborhood with substantial force—no pumps required. This is why many cities, especially older ones, were designed around elevated reservoirs and water towers. The water in the tower is doing the work of pumping, for free, every hour of the day.
